questions.q: According to Robbins and Coulter, organizing means determining:
o: What tasks are done, who does them, how they are grouped, who reports to whom and where decisions are made
Only how much each employee is paid
questions.d: Organizing (Robbins & Coulter): determining tasks, who does them, how they are grouped, reporting relationships and where decisions are made.
questions.w: Organizing is about arranging work and authority, not pay, strategy or advertising.

questions.q: L.A. Allen's definition of organizing includes identifying and grouping work and:
o: Defining and delegating responsibility and authority, and establishing relationships
questions.d: Organizing (L.A. Allen): identifying and grouping work, defining and delegating responsibility and authority, and establishing relationships so people work effectively together.
questions.w: Recruiting is staffing and measuring performance is controlling.

questions.q: Organization structure is best described as:
o: The outcome of the organizing process and a framework of decision-making authority
A list of the company's customers
questions.d: Organization structure: the outcome of organizing; a framework of decision-making authority and a system of relationships governing people's activities.
questions.w: It shows how authority and relationships are arranged to achieve goals.

questions.q: What is the FIRST step in developing an organization structure?
o: Revising the system based on personnel and funds
questions.d: Steps: 1 define objectives clearly, 2 identify and group activities, 3 determine the structure, 4 revise based on personnel and funds.
questions.w: Objectives determine the type and basic characteristics of the organization, so they come first.

questions.q: The span of supervision (span of control) is:
o: The number of subordinates a manager can effectively manage
The number of departments in a company
The length of the chain of command
questions.d: Span of control: the number of subordinates a manager can effectively manage; it decides whether the organization is flat or tall.
questions.w: A wide span gives a flat structure; a narrow span gives a tall one.

questions.q: Departmentation is:
o: The process of grouping activities into units for administration at all levels
questions.d: Departmentation: grouping activities into units for administration, dividing personnel and functions into separate units.
questions.w: It is the 'grouping' part of organizing.

questions.q: Putting similar and related activities under one department is which factor in departmentation?
questions.d: Factors in departmentation: specialization, facilitating control, facilitating coordination, balance, reduction of cost.
questions.w: Grouping similar activities builds specialised knowledge, which is specialization.

questions.q: Grouping activities to avoid repetition and cut financial cost is which factor?
questions.d: Reduction of cost: activities grouped to best achieve objectives at lower cost, e.g. by avoiding repetition.
questions.w: Avoiding duplication saves money.

questions.q: The most widely used form of departmentation is by:
questions.d: Functional structure: groups activities into major functional departments; the most widely used.
questions.w: Basic functions are production, selling and financing, plus buying, accounting, personnel and research.

questions.q: The basic functions in a functional structure are usually classified into:
questions.d: Functional structure: basic functions are production, selling and financing.
questions.w: Planning, organizing and controlling are management functions, not departments.

questions.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of a functional structure?
o: It ensures specialization and coordination within each function
It is a good training ground for all-round managers
It speeds up all decisions through decentralization
It removes the need for coordination
questions.d: Functional advantages: specialization, coordination within the function, adequate attention to basic activities; a time-proved method.
questions.w: A functional company is NOT a good training ground for all-round managers, and it tends to centralize decisions.

questions.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of a functional structure?
o: Excessive centralization delays decisions and the flow of information
High administrative cost from project teams
questions.d: Functional disadvantages: excessive centralization causing delay, executives focused narrowly on their own function, poor training for all-round managers.
questions.w: Two chains of command and high administrative costs belong to the matrix structure.

questions.q: In a divisional (product) structure:
o: One executive is in charge of all activities for a product or product line
Each employee serves only one specialist function
All decisions are made by the CEO
questions.d: Divisional structure: activities for each product or product line are combined into integrated units, each led by an executive with extensive authority.
questions.w: The location of the product unit is irrelevant in this structure.

questions.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of a divisional structure?
o: Product lines can be compared, so unprofitable ones can be dropped and profitable ones expanded
It has no coordination problems at all
It gives every employee two chains of command
questions.d: Divisional advantages: specialised product knowledge, motivated product managers, comparison of product lines, better coordination and customer service.
questions.w: Each product's results are separate, which makes comparison easy.

questions.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of a divisional structure?
o: Top management may find it hard to monitor and control the various product departments
Too much centralization in functional departments
questions.d: Divisional disadvantages: coordination difficulties, control problems for top management, and reluctance to delegate decisions to departmental heads.
questions.w: Many semi-independent divisions are harder for top management to monitor.

questions.q: A matrix structure is a combination of:
o: Functional and divisional structures, with vertical and horizontal chains of command
questions.d: Matrix structure: imposes horizontal divisional reporting on a hierarchical functional structure; two chains of command.
questions.w: Employees report both to a functional manager (vertical) and a project or product manager (horizontal).

questions.q: The matrix structure is also known as:
o: Grid organization or project/product management organization
questions.d: Matrix structure: also known as grid organization or project or product management organization.
questions.w: The grid shape comes from its two crossing lines of authority.

questions.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of a matrix structure?
o: Flexible use of manpower and other resources
questions.d: Matrix advantages: decentralised decisions, better project coordination, better response to change, flexible use of resources.
questions.w: Matrix structures actually have high administrative costs and confusion over authority.

questions.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of a matrix structure?
o: Confusion over authority and conflict about who reports to whom
questions.d: Matrix disadvantages: high administrative costs, confusion over authority and responsibility, interpersonal conflict, overemphasis on group decision-making.
questions.w: Two bosses can give conflicting instructions, causing power struggles.

questions.q: In a centralized organization, major decisions are made:
o: At the top by the CEO and carried out by everyone below
By managers at all levels for daily operations
questions.d: Centralization: major decisions are made at the top. Decentralization: day-to-day decisions are made by managers at various levels.
questions.w: The essential difference between the two is where decisions are made.

questions.q: Which is a reason organizations need decentralization?
o: To reduce the burden on top executives
To keep all power with the CEO
questions.d: Need for decentralization: reduce top executives' burden, diversify product lines, focus on product markets, develop future managers, raise morale, keep pace with technology.
questions.w: Sharing decisions frees top executives to focus on major issues.

questions.q: Line functions are those that:
o: Have direct responsibility for accomplishing the organization's objectives
Only give advice to other managers
Handle only office cleaning and security
questions.d: Line functions: direct responsibility for objectives. Staff: help the line work more effectively.
questions.w: For example, production and sales are line; legal advice or HR support are staff.

questions.q: Which describes a STAFF manager?
o: Assists others and provides specialised guidance and ideas to the line
Has final responsibility for achieving objectives
questions.d: Staff managers assist, investigate problems, solve special problems, make plans and provide ideas and specialised guidance.
questions.w: Veto power, final responsibility and operating decisions belong to line managers.

questions.q: Which describes a LINE manager?
o: A generalist who directs others and has final responsibility for achieving objectives
A specialist who only investigates problems
questions.d: Line managers: generalists who direct others, delegate authority, use sanctions, have veto power and final responsibility.
questions.w: The line has direct authority; staff supports it.

questions.q: A matrix structure has only one chain of command.
questions.d: Matrix structure: two chains of command, vertical (functional) and horizontal (divisional/project).
questions.w: Having two bosses is what makes the matrix structure different.

questions.q: A functionally organized company is a good training ground for all-round promotable managers.
questions.d: A disadvantage of functional structure: it does not offer a good training ground for all-round managers.
questions.w: Managers specialise in one function, so they do not learn the whole business.

questions.q: In a divisional (product) structure, the place or location of the product unit is irrelevant.
questions.d: Divisional by product: activities are grouped by product; place or location is irrelevant.
questions.w: The grouping is based on products, not geography.

questions.q: Matrix structures require high administrative costs.
questions.d: Matrix disadvantages include high administrative costs.
questions.w: Running two lines of authority needs more managers and coordination.

questions.q: In decentralization, the CEO sets guidelines, but day-to-day decisions are made by managers at various levels.
questions.d: Decentralization: the CEO sets the tone and guidelines; managers at different levels make day-to-day decisions.
questions.w: This spreads decision-making down the organization.

questions.q: Revising the system based on an assessment of personnel and funds is a step in developing an organization structure.
questions.d: Step 4: revise the system based on the capacities of available people and other resources.
questions.w: A structure must fit the people and money actually available.

questions.q: Define organizing and organization structure.
questions.a:
Organizing (Robbins & Coulter): determining what tasks are to be done, who is to do them, how the tasks are grouped, who reports to whom, and where decisions are made.
Organizing (L.A. Allen): identifying and grouping work, defining and delegating responsibility and authority, and establishing relationships so people work effectively together.
Organization structure: the outcome of the organizing process; a framework of decision-making authority and a system of relationships that governs people's activities to achieve goals. Key executives determine it.
questions.d: Organizing is the process; organization structure is its outcome.
questions.w: Give a definition of each term and show how they are linked.

questions.q: Explain the four steps in developing an organization structure.
questions.a:
1. Clear definition of objectives: they determine the type and basic characteristics of the organization.
2. Identifying the activities and grouping them: list the activities needed to achieve objectives, group them systematically and assign them to personnel.
3. Determining the structure: decide the span of control (flat or tall), type of organization, basis of departmentation and pattern of authority.
4. Revising the system: assess the capacities of the people available and other resources (funds) and adjust.
questions.d: Organization structure: a framework of authority and relationships.
questions.w: The steps move from purpose (objectives) to work, then to structure, then to fitting it to resources.

questions.q: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of a functional structure.
questions.a:
Functional structure: groups activities into major functional departments (production, selling, financing, plus buying, accounting, personnel, research). It is the most widely used.
Advantages:
- Ensures specialization and specialised knowledge and skill.
- Facilitates coordination within each function.
- Gives adequate attention to the basic activities.
- A time-proved method that management can justify.
Disadvantages:
- Excessive centralization delays decisions and information flow.
- Executives become too focused on their own functional areas.
- Not a good training ground for all-round promotable managers.
questions.d: Functional structure: departmentation by functions, where each employee serves a specialist role.
questions.w: Strength and weakness come from the same source: deep specialization within functions.

questions.q: Explain the divisional structure and its advantages and disadvantages.
questions.a:
Divisional structure: activities for each product or product line are combined into integrated units, each led by an executive with authority over production, sales, development and service. Location is irrelevant.
Advantages:
- Specialised product knowledge and coordination of product activities.
- Product managers are motivated to expand and improve their product.
- Product lines can be compared (drop unprofitable, expand profitable).
- Better coordination, customer service and control of resources.
Disadvantages:
- Coordination difficulties.
- Control problems for top management monitoring many product departments.
- Top management may be unwilling to delegate decision-making to departmental heads.
questions.d: Divisional structure: departmentation by product or service.
questions.w: Each division works like a small business, which helps focus but makes central control harder.

questions.q: Explain the matrix structure with its advantages and disadvantages.
questions.a:
Matrix structure: a combination of functional and divisional structures. It imposes horizontal divisional reporting on a vertical functional hierarchy, so employees have two chains of command. Also called grid, project or product management organization.
Advantages:
- Decentralised decision-making.
- Better project or product coordination.
- Better monitoring of, and response to, environmental change.
- Flexible use of manpower and other resources.
Disadvantages:
- High administrative costs.
- Confusion over authority and responsibility (power struggles).
- More interpersonal conflict (who reports to whom?).
- Overemphasis on group decision-making.
questions.d: Matrix structure: two chains of command, vertical and horizontal.
questions.w: The double reporting line gives flexibility but also creates confusion and conflict.

questions.q: Distinguish between line and staff managers.
questions.a:
Line functions have direct responsibility for accomplishing objectives; staff help the line work more effectively.
Line managers:
- Generalists who direct others and delegate authority.
- Train subordinates, use sanctions and exert control.
- Have veto power and take operating decisions.
- Have final responsibility for achieving objectives.
Staff managers:
- Specialists who assist others and serve authority.
- Investigate and solve special problems and make plans.
- Support the line and provide ideas.
- Provide specialised guidance to achieve objectives.
questions.d: Line authority: direct command. Staff authority: advisory and supportive.
questions.w: Line managers decide and command; staff managers advise and support.
